_why: Milestone 0.4. rule-diff.sh reports every per-rule count change between the
last release and this build. Reporting is not accountability: a drop and a
correct narrowing look identical in that output, and the only thing telling
them apart was whoever happened to read the job summary.
This file is the other half. Every rule whose count DROPS must have an entry
here saying why. An unexplained drop fails the job; so does an entry that no
longer describes a real drop, because a ledger nothing validates rots into
The baseline is the last released nox, so entries accumulate between releases
and are cleared when one is cut. `nox_release` records which release they are
written against: if it does not match the tag rule-diff resolved, the ledger
is stale as a whole and says so rather than silently passing.

classifications.duplicate-retired: a second rule reported the same condition; one ID was retired into the other, which carries the alias
classifications.applicability-narrowed: the rule does not apply to this subject or resource kind, and now says so
classifications.sanitizer-recognized: the value reaching the sink is neutralized for this vulnerability class
classifications.refined-away: a cheaper semantic fact refutes the candidate the pattern generated
classifications.rule-removed: the rule was deleted outright; no survivor reports the condition
classifications.context-narrowed: the rule's context requirement is now measured in characters as well as lines, so a keyword far away on the same physical line no longer qualifies as context
classifications.keyword-tokenized: the rule's vendor keyword must now be a token; it used to match as a bare substring, so it could be supplied by an accident inside opaque data or by an ordinary English word
classifications.format-bound: the rule now requires the vendor's real credential format; the value it matched is issued by that vendor but is not a credential
classifications.binding-required: the vendor name must now BIND the value through an assignment; sitting adjacent to a generic token is not evidence that the token is that vendor's credential

entries.reason: The response side and the bodies of a recorded HTTP exchange are traffic, not a credential the repository holds — and nobody can rotate them. Measured on crewAI 1.15.21 against v1.35.0, SEC-161 and SEC-162 produced 540 findings and every one was inside a vcrpy cassette: 202 __cf_bm and 32 _cfuvid Cloudflare cookies, 148 continuation lines of base64 response bodies, 58 response ids, 44 embedding vectors up to 8,193 characters, 32 Gemini thought signatures, and 8 occurrences of PostHog's phc_ project key, which the vendor publishes and SEC-661 deliberately excludes. SEC-161 fell 522 to 0 on that repository and is unchanged everywhere else in the corpus. The gate covers the entropy rules only: any rule encoding a vendor's credential format still fires anywhere in a recording, including a request body, which is where an OAuth client_secret sits. The request headers and URI are untouched, and SEC-082 was fixed in the same change so that an unredacted authorization header in a cassette is reported at all — it was not, because Go's \s crosses a newline but not a YAML sequence dash. See docs/design/recorded-http-exchanges.md.

Same gate as SEC-161: the bodies and response side of a recorded HTTP exchange are server traffic. 18 to 0 on crewAI. See that entry for the measured breakdown and for the false negative fixed alongside it.

Re-keyed from `live_[a-zA-Z0-9]{32}` near the word "checkout" onto Checkout.com's documented prefixes `sk_` and `sk_sbox_`. The old pattern matched no Checkout.com key of any kind and did match any `live_` token near a word that appears in e-commerce code constantly. pk_ is deliberately absent: Checkout.com publishes the public key for client-side use, and reporting a credential the vendor documents as publishable trains people to ignore the rule, which is the reason SEC-661 omits PostHog's phc_. Stripe's `sk_live_`/`sk_test_` namespace (SEC-030) cannot collide, because `[a-z0-9]{26,}` cannot cross the underscore — asserted by TestSEC562DoesNotClaimStripesNamespace, which was checked by breaking that property.

Removed. SEC-572 "Payoneer API Token" matched `live_[a-zA-Z0-9]{32}`, and Payoneer issues no credential of that shape: it authenticates with OAuth2 client_id/client_secret and publishes no token prefix, length or charset at all. A rule cannot encode a format the vendor does not have. It shared the pattern with SEC-562, so one token near either vendor name produced a finding named for the other; SEC-562 was re-keyed onto Checkout.com's real prefixes and SEC-572 had nothing to be re-keyed onto. No survivor reports "a Payoneer token" because nothing distinguishes one from any other OAuth client secret; a hardcoded client secret is still reported by the generic credential rules, which is the correct strength of claim.

Two classes v1.39.2 did not cover. (1) Python docstrings: v1.39.2 gated the JavaScript extractor on lexctx so prose in a comment stopped being collected as an import, and left the Python extractor ungated — and a docstring showing a caller what to type is the most common place in Python to write an import you are not making. Same gate, same keyword offset, same reasoning. (2) An interpolated specifier: no npm registry can serve a name containing `$`, `{` or `}`, so `@ai-sdk/${pkgName}` and `${moduleName}` are not package names and reporting them undeclared asserts a hallucinated package on the strength of a code generator. The lexctx gate already catches the common shape, where the generated import sits inside a template literal; this covers the rest of the class exactly rather than heuristically. The control test keeps JSONStream and lodash.debounce resolving, because a false negative here is silent.

AI-019 "Model loaded without hash verification" matched `from_pretrained(` and stopped at the opening paren, so it never saw the arguments; its own comment conceded this and argued the absence was still the signal because a pinned line was "unlikely to match". A pinned load was reported exactly like an unpinned one, so the rule's name asserted something its pattern had not established. excludeContextKeywords now establishes it, and reaches a multi-line call where widening the pattern would not. Of 99 model loads across the fourteen pinned repositories, ZERO carry a pin, so no count is expected to move: the rule was right about every one of them for a reason it could not give, and what the gate buys is that a project which does pin stops being told it has not. The same change fixes a false negative in the other direction — a bare `pipeline("sentiment-analysis")` as the first token on a line matched nothing, because the character class excluding `conn.pipeline()` needs a character.
